text.tspan: Everyday English - C2 - 2026/04/18 - Essay - 01
Hands cultivate a garden with care.
Pexels · 7729129
Earth Day in everyday choices
To reduce everyday waste is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the contingencies of shared
experience. The question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position supports preparation while
withholding the assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: changing one repeat purchase can reduce waste over time. Here, we bring a reusable bag and refill a bottle. The
arrangement earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity to an abstract ideal of order. Its success is
consequently conditional. Once the intervention demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the original justification begins to unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since local knowledge makes shared action more effective. In
concrete terms, we check the local recycling rules before sorting materials. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose convenience supplies the
standard against which improvement is measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its designer. Attentiveness to others
makes that asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience
without exhausting its meaning. Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life
more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life must conform.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body paragraph
needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Compare two ways to reduce everyday waste: a rigid plan and one that allows adjustment. Assess one advantage and one limitation. Use four short
paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss changing one repeat
purchase can reduce waste over time with an example; discuss local knowledge makes shared action more effective with a different example; conclude
by connecting the two points.)
